title: Cushion-led Burst Orchestrator & Fallback Playbook (PRD - rough)
content:
Summary:

This PRD describes a thin, operationally-friendly approach to handling tenant microbursts and long-tail demand in Dedicated capacity: the Cushion-led Burst Orchestrator (CBO). The primary goal is to give tenants predictable tail-latency and SLO behavior while maximizing overall GPU utilization and providing clear, auditable fallback behavior when capacity is constrained.

Problem statement:

Current dedicated pools face three recurring tradeoffs:
- Tenants want low p99 latency during short spikes but buying large reserved pools is expensive.
- Static burst credit systems either overcommit (hurting p99) or underutilize resources (wasting money).
- Operational complexity increases when we combine preemption, soft-failover to hosted models, and fairness across tenants with different SLOs.

Design principles:

1) Safety-first: never violate tenant-declared hard SLOs (when contractually guaranteed) without a clear, repairable fallback.
2) Predictability: observable cushion metrics and explicit decay/payback policies so customers can reason about burst behavior.
3) Simplicity for users: a small surface of knobs (cushion_target, burst_mode, payback_policy) with strong defaults.
4) Operator-friendly: deterministic runbooks and simulation harness for validating configuration changes.

Key concepts and components:

- Cushion (soft reserve): a small per-tenant kept buffer expressed in concurrency or GPU-minutes that is replenished according to a decay/payback schedule. Think of it as a per-tenant safety margin that privileges short spikes.

- Burst lanes: transient channels that allow tenants to exceed their committed steady-state capacity using Cushion. Burst lanes are classified:
  * elastic: best-effort, shared across tenants, reclaimed under pressure (low-cost).
  * committed-burst: reserved at time of purchase or billing commitment (higher-cost, stronger guarantees).
  * isolated-fastlane: gated to protect latency-critical workflows; has the strictest fallback rules (onboarding required).

- Cushion Ledger & Payback: the system tracks cushion consumption in a ledger. Payback policies are pluggable: linear decay, exponential decay, or usage-weighted (default linear over 1h). The ledger is auditable and is surfaced to customers in console.

- Soft Preempt & Grace Windows: when reclaiming capacity, tenants in elastic lanes enter a configurable grace window (default 30s) during which requests receive slowdown signals (503 with Retry-After or throttled tokens) before hard preemption. This reduces tail surprises.

- Fallback routing: deterministic routing policies that decide whether to fall back to: a) a lower-capacity compatible model variant, b) Hosted API (with explicit billing fallback), or c) queued-then-retry within the cushion grace window.

Customer configuration surface:

Expose 3 primary knobs in Console / API:
- cushion_target: numeric, GPU-minutes or concurrent-runners; default small (10% of committed).
- burst_mode: [elastic | committed-burst | isolate-fastlane]. Default: elastic.
- payback_policy: [linear:3600, exponential:900, weighted]. Default: linear:3600 (seconds).

Example API (user-facing config snippet):
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-inc-1",
  "cushion_target": "0.1x_commit",
  "burst_mode": "elastic",
  "payback_policy": "linear:3600"
}

Observability & metrics:

Surface via Console and traces:
- cushion_utilization (percent of cushion in use), 1m/5m/1h windows
- spill_rate (requests rejected due to cushion exhaustion)
- payback_velocity (rate at which cushion is refilled)
- fallback_rate (how often flow fell back to hosted or degraded model)
- p50/p90/p99 by model and by burst_mode
- per-tenant ledger history (time-series of cushion consumption)

SLOs / Billing / Economics:

- Default billing: cushion consumption billed at a delta premium (e.g., 1.5x tokens-to-cost) when used beyond committed capacity in elastic lanes; committed-burst pricing negotiated.
- Introduce a visible "cushion burn" statement in invoices with timestamps and payback adjustments.
- Provide a simulation tool (bench-sim v2) to estimate cushion burn under historical traffic.

Operator runbook (high-level):

1) Detection: automated alert when pool-level cushion_utilization > 75% for 15m, or when spill_rate spikes > baseline.
2) Initial mitigation: enable temporary global conservative-throttle (soft limit) and push targeted tenant notifications.
3) If pressure persists: identify top-consuming tenants via ledger; request tenant teams to increase cushion_target or shift to committed-burst lanes.
4) Emergency: execute documented failover to hosted fallback for affected tenants (audit log + customer notification).

Simulation & validation plan:

- Build bench-sim v2 scenarios using production traces: diurnal spikes, sudden 10x microbursts, holiday-season surges.
- Run A/B: baseline (current credit system) vs. CBO with default params. Metrics: p99 latency, GPU utilization, number of fallbacks, and invoice deltas.

Rollout strategy:

Phase 0: internal dogfood with product and SRE on a single pool (2–3 tenants) for 6 weeks.
Phase 1: opt-in public beta for existing Dedicated customers (billing flagged, clear console opt-in) for 8 weeks.
Phase 2: default-on for new tenants with migration tooling and auto-simulation to suggest cushion_target.

Experiment matrix (examples):
- Vary cushion size: 5%, 10%, 20% of commit -> measure p99 and burn rate.
- Test payback_policy: linear vs exponential -> measure fairness when adjacent bursts occur.
- Compare fallback destinations: hosted vs model-variant -> customer-visible latency and cost impacts.

Open questions & risks:

- Pricing sensitivity: will customers accept surcharges for cushion consumption? Need sales feedback and legal review.
- Multi-tenant fairness: even with cushion led approach, pathological tenants could game the ledger; consider soft quotas and anomaly detectors.
- Observability cost: storing high-resolution ledger history for thousands of tenants has storage/ingest cost.

Action items / next steps:

- Engineering: prototype Cushion Ledger and grace-window reclamation in the staging serving-runtime (owner: Diego).
- Product: finalize default knob values and console UX (owner: Claire).
- SRE/Finance: draft billing experiment and invoice line-item design (owners: Evan + Priya).
- Legal: review contractual language for fallback to hosted models and surcharges.

Appendix (runbook snippets):

- Quick mitigation checklist:
  * Alert triage -> identify top tenants -> flip pool-level soft-limit to 70% -> notify tenant contact -> if no relief in 30m, escalate to emergency fallback.

- Example customer message (automated):
  "We observed sustained burst usage that exhausted cushion resources in pool X. To avoid hard preemption, traffic may be routed to a lower-latency model or temporarily limited. Contact your account team to increase cushion or switch to committed-burst."

This document is intentionally prescriptive and operational — the goal is to ship a low cognitive-overhead default that reduces surprise during spikes while keeping economics transparent.
summary: Draft PRD for Cushion-led Burst Orchestrator: a per-tenant soft-reserve, burst lanes, payback ledger, grace windows, and deterministic fallback policies to balance latency guarantees and utilization in Dedicated pools.
